item.research_question: How does laser remelting affect the surface properties of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy?
item.processing_route: Laser remelting with a laser power of 4 kW, laser spot size of 30 mm × 2 mm, and scanning rates of 5 mm·s−1
item.test_conditions: Dry-sliding tribological tests with a sliding velocity of 0.28 m·s−1, a sliding time of 30 min, and a normal load of 500 g
key_findings: The microstructure of the remelted layer transformed into a fine basket-weave morphology consisting of the FCC phase and BCC phase
The Vickers microhardness of the HEA increased from 271 HV to 483 HV, with a 78% increment
The average friction coefficient and the wear rate of the remelted alloy were minimized by 23% and 80%, respectively, compared with the as-cast HEA
The remelted layer maintained considerable plasticity with a high Wp/Wt ratio (0.763) and a strain hardening exponent (0.302)
item.mechanism: The ultra-fast cooling rate of the LR process led to a significant rise in the surface hardness of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA, and the reduction in adhesive wear contributed to the lower friction coefficient and wear rate of the remelted layer
item.future_work: The findings of this study may provide the theoretical and technical basis for the laser additive manufacturing of the AlxCoCrFeNi HEA
quotes: The laser remelting technique was applied to the surface modification of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) to further advance its mechanical potential
The microstructure of the remelted layer was refined from coarse dendritic to submicron-scale basket weave compared with the as-cast substrate

records.text: Paper card. Question: How does laser remelting affect the surface properties of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy?. System: Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy. Processing: Laser remelting with a laser power of 4 kW, laser spot size of 30 mm × 2 mm, and scanning rates of 5 mm·s−1. Test conditions: Dry-sliding tribological tests with a sliding velocity of 0.28 m·s−1, a sliding time of 30 min, and a normal load of 500 g. Findings: The microstructure of the remelted layer transformed into a fine basket-weave morphology consisting of the FCC phase and BCC phase; The Vickers microhardness of the HEA increased from 271 HV to 483 HV, with a 78% increment; The average friction coefficient and the wear rate of the remelted alloy were minimized by 23% and 80%, respectively, compared with the as-cast HEA; The remelted layer maintained considerable plasticity with a high Wp/Wt ratio (0.763) and a strain hardening exponent (0.302). Mechanism: The ultra-fast cooling rate of the LR process led to a significant rise in the surface hardness of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA, and the reduction in adhesive wear contributed to the lower friction coefficient and wear rate of the remelted layer. Future work: The findings of this study may provide the theoretical and technical basis for the laser additive manufacturing of the AlxCoCrFeNi HEA. Quote: "The laser remelting technique was applied to the surface modification of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) to further advance its mechanical potential"
